title: The Market Ledger
subject: Excel
intro: Tove's trading post keeps its accounts in a spreadsheet, but the totals are missing. Write real formulas to work out revenue, totals and averages.

objectives.label: Find values by their cell address
Write formulas that calculate from cells
Use functions such as SUM and AVERAGE on ranges
Know when to fix a reference with $

badge.name: Ledger Keeper
badge.description: Built working spreadsheet formulas instead of typing in answers.

takeaway: Formulas refer to cells, not typed numbers, so they update when the data changes. Ranges like B2:B5 feed functions such as SUM and AVERAGE, and a $ fixes a reference when you fill a formula down.

scenes.title: The harbour market
scenes.speaker: tove
lines: Fresh furs, Baltic amber, honey from the hills! Oh, you're the Pathfinder Mira mentioned.
My spreadsheet lists what I sold this week, but I never worked out the money. I just guess.
Teach me to let the spreadsheet do the sums, and I'll stop guessing.

scenes.title: Finding your way around
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Every cell has an address: its column letter, then its row number.
scenes.code:
A        B       C
1  Item     Price   Qty sold
2  Furs       25       6
3  Honey       8      15
4  Amber      40       3
5  Rope        5      22
scenes.prompt: Which cell holds the price of Honey?

options.feedback: Yes. Price is column B and Honey is on row 3, so B3 holds 8.
C3 is Honey's quantity sold (15). Price is in column B.
B2 is the price of Furs. Honey is one row down.
A3 holds the word Honey itself. The price is to its right.

hints: Column letter first, then row number.
Find the Price column, then go down to Honey's row.
scenes.explanation: A cell address is column letter + row number, like B3. Formulas use these addresses to read values.

scenes.title: Revenue per item
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Revenue is price times quantity. Write it once and the spreadsheet fills it down for the other items.
scenes.prompt: Type a formula in D2 that calculates revenue for Furs. It will be filled down to D5.
scenes.successFeedback: All four revenues are right: 150, 120, 120 and 110.
hints: Formulas start with =, then use cell addresses instead of numbers.
Furs' price is in B2 and its quantity in C2. Multiply them with *.
scenes.explanation: =B2*C2 multiplies two cells. When it's filled down, Excel shifts the row numbers (B3*C3, B4*C4…), which is why referring to cells beats typing numbers.

scenes.title: The week's total
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Now the most important number: how much did I take in altogether?
scenes.prompt: Type a formula in D6 that adds up all the revenue in D2 to D5.
hints: SUM adds up a range of cells.
A range is written first:last, like D2:D5.
scenes.explanation: =SUM(D2:D5) adds every cell from D2 to D5. If a sale is corrected, the total updates by itself, unlike =150+120+120+110.

scenes.title: The average price
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: A customer asked what my goods cost on average.
scenes.prompt: Type a formula in B6 that calculates the average price of the four items.
hints: There's a function named after exactly what you want.
=AVERAGE(…) with the range of prices, B2 to B5.
scenes.explanation: AVERAGE adds a range and divides by how many numbers it contains. Choosing the right range matters as much as the right function.

scenes.title: The fixed tax rate
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: The harbour tax rate (10%) is in cell F1. Tove typed =D2*F1 in E2 and filled it down. E2 is right, but E3, E4 and E5 all show 0.
scenes.prompt: What's going wrong, and how do you fix it?

options.text: Filling down shifted F1 to F2, F3…, which are empty. Use $F$1 to keep it fixed
options.feedback: Exactly. $ before the column and row locks the reference, so every row uses the tax rate in F1.

options.text: 10% should be typed into every row of column F
options.feedback: That works, but copying the rate everywhere means changing it in many places later. A fixed reference is the better fix.
SUM adds things up. Tax is revenue times the rate, so * is right. The reference is the problem.

options.text: The spreadsheet is broken. Retype the formula in each cell
options.feedback: Nothing is broken. Excel did exactly what relative references do when filled down.

hints: Look at how the formula changes from row 2 to row 3.
Which reference should stay the same on every row?
scenes.explanation: Relative references (F1) shift when filled; absolute references ($F$1) don't. Use $ for single settings like a tax rate that every row should share.

scenes.title: The books balance
scenes.speaker: tove
lines: 500 for the week! And if I fix a sale, every number updates by itself.
No more guessing. The spreadsheet does the sums and I check they make sense.
The steward in the Great Hall wants a proper dashboard. You're ready for it.
